Just wondering what everyone is doing to protect themselves from this. Most of my clients are short on resources, therefore I am implementing SRP (Software restriction policies, GPO) and doing some due diligence in testing their applications, and whitelisting what needs to be run from their Appdata and user directories.

However, I'm interested in hearing what others are doing.
What are you doing against Crypto?
Nothing. As soon as someone is infected, we nuke the computer and restore from backup.
Remove their access. Send them to training. Wipe comp.
killed exe from appdata type of gpo to prevent infection. User training emails, user training emails, user training emails. When found we nuke from orbit as that is the only way to be sure.

Make sure backups are good. App locker. Security audits to make sure people don't have access to stuff they don't need. Spam policies (especially that resume.zip thing going around since it was getting by filters for a little bit). But the most important part has been user training. I keep up on security blogs, and every time a new wave hits, I make sure to update users and remind them that they are not to open attachments they aren't expecting. Out of the 200 clients I have, this last wave affected zero, I think because we let them know about the resume.zip trick and reminded them about suspicions emails.

I have been using WaniKani for a couple of weeks now and in my opinion it's one of the best places to learn kanji. It uses a Spaced Repetition System. This is how it roughly works:

First you learn some radicals, the building blocks of kanji. After you show that you have them memorized, by correctly answering reviews, you unlock some kanji. And when you do the kanji reviews correctly, you unlock some vocabulary that uses the kanji.

I am sure people here can explain it better than me, but this is roughly the gist of it.

If you wanna try it, go to http://www.wanikani.com/ the first two levels are free. One level takes about a week of your time, if you answer everything 100% correct. This gives you about two weeks to see if it is something you are interested in and/or to see if it works for you. After that you have to subscribe to continue.

I can probably answer some things here, but do check out the website if it seems interesting!
Thank you, I will try it out.

I thought it was very good, but I got stuck on a couple of issues that made me move to another app.

-They had different names for radicals and the individual kanji of that single radical. I can't remember the specific items, maybe industry, cross or something else? I would always get them confused, which would reset my progress on that item. I could never understand why they would invent a name for a radical that had a different meaning in kanji form.

-If I made a mistake with the onyomi or kunyomi, it would reset my progress on the whole word. It seemed like there were two or three words that I could never progress on because I would make that stupid mistake. It seemed like I could never progress beyond that level as a result. I couldn't figure out how to just focus on those two items and learn them really well so I could move on. I always had to go through a very long list of things I already knew only to get tripped up again by those two or three items.

I felt like it was a great resource to learn the radicals, readings and meaning. I really wish I could have contacted the devs through the app to give feedback. I was really getting a lot out of it until I ran into those blocks.

That was a few months ago. Since then, I have been using Anki, which has a similar repetition system. It certainly doesn't have the breadth of wanikani since it is only a flash card app, but it allows for more options to really drill down problematic cards.
